list.listitem: The range of presentation is highly variable, and many patients present as adults with infertility. Klinefelter syndrome is underdiagnosed, and clinicians should be mindful of the syndrome when examining well children and adults. C
The gold standard for diagnosis is cytogenetic analysis (XXY karyotype most common). C
Infertility is rapidly progressive during adolescence and early adulthood. When appropriate, patients should undergo semen analysis and cryopreservation of sperm. C
Patients are at increased risk for diabetes, osteoporosis, breast cancer, and cardiovascular disease; screening should be considered. C

Testosterone supplementation in patients with hypogonadal Klinefelter syndrome has benefits on body composition and bone density and may improve mood and behavioral functioning; potential benefits and risks should be discussed with patients. B

background.definition: Klinefelter syndrome is a genetic syndrome characterized by male gender with more than one X chromosome (e.g., 47XXY, 48XXXY, and so forth) in many or all body cells. Most (90%) men have the XXY karyotype.

list.listitem: 1.5 to 2 per 1000 men
0.02%−0.22% of the general US population
Klinefelter syndrome is the most common sex chromosome disorder, but only approximately 25% to 50% of cases are diagnosed, and only 4% to 10% are diagnosed before puberty.

Individuals who are transgender appear to have a higher prevalence of Klinefelter syndrome than the general population; in one systematic review including 1376 transgender individuals, 1.02% were diagnosed with Klinefelter syndrome and 9/1013 (0.88%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.4%-1.7%) had confirmation based on karyotyping.
Klinefelter syndrome accounts for 3% of male infertility and is a common cause of otherwise undifferentiated mental retardation.

Increased prevalence of cardiovascular abnormalities is found in patients with Klinefelter syndrome including abnormalities in left ventricular systolic and diastolic function, endothelial function and increased risk of atrial fibrillation (but not stroke).

Authors of a Swedish population study found higher rates of the following cancers in patients with Klinefelter syndrome compared to the general population: hematological malignancy (standardized incidence ratio [SIR] = 2.7), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (SIR = 3.0), breast cancer (SIR = 4.4), and leukemia (SIR = 3.6).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies found a pooled prevalence of 28% (95% CI: 19%-36%) for erectile dysfunction and 51% (95% CI: 36%-66%) for decreased libido, although there was large study heterogeneity.

Patients with Klinefelter syndrome experience higher rates of mood disorders than the general population. In one multi-center cross-sectional study including 219 men with Klinefelter syndrome, 18% reported chronic anxiety, 16.6% chronic depression and 27.3% sometimes or often had suicidal thoughts.
Gender dysphoria may be more prevalent in patients with Klinefelter syndrome than for males in the general population.

There appears to be an increased prevalence of ADHD in individuals with Klinefelter syndrome compared to the general population. Pharmacological treatment for ADHD appears to be effective and well-tolerated.
Caused by meiotic nondisjunction of X chromosome during gametogenesis; in the case of mosaic Klinefelter syndrome, nondisjunction occurs during mitosis of the zygote.
Approximately 90% of patients have the XXY karyotype; 10% have the mosaic 47XXY/46XY karyotype or other karyotypes such as 48XXXY.
Patients have low or low-normal testosterone, and high or high-normal gonadotropins (follicle-stimulating hormone and leuteinizing hormone).
It is frequently unclear which characteristics of the disease are caused by hypogonadism, which are mediated by presence of an additional X chromosome, and which are a combined effect.

Testicular fibrosis leads to development of azoospermia and infertility, but the cause of this is unknown. Based on a literature review, hypotheses on mechanism(s) causing the fibrosis include the influence of altered Sertoli cells on germ cells, the hormonal impact on Leydig cells, the inflammation mediated by mast cells, fibrous extracellular matrix deposition by peritubular myoid cells, and the possible role of the altered microvasculature.

Low bone mineral density seen in some patients with Klinefelter syndrome may be due in part to testicular hormone effects on sclerostin, an osteocyte-specific protein that negatively regulates bone formation.

Altered neurogenesis, gliogenesis, and glutamate signaling pathways have been demonstrated and may contribute to the abnormal brain development and later cognitive phenotypes in individuals with Klinefelter syndrome. In a small case control study, boys with Klinefelter syndrome had reduced executive function compared to typically developing boys and the magnitude of activation differences on functional MRI was associated with severity of pubertal developmental delay.
Characteristic physical and cognitive features are highly variable in presentation.
As the number of X chromosome increases, the phenotypic severity of the disease increases.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Maternal age: 30-34 years (comparison: younger than 25 years)

list.listitem: Men with Klinefelter syndrome have an increased risk of breast cancer compared with other men (RR = 20-62), although the RR is much lower when compared with women of the same age (RR = 0.14 or less). The median age of diagnosis is 72 years, and no cases were found in patients younger than 50 years in a large population study. There are no evidence-based screening recommendations, but low-risk screening methods (annual clinical examination) should be considered and men should be encouraged to report breast masses. C

Mortality from diabetes and cardiovascular disease is increased. Periodic diabetes screening is recommended. C Diabetes frequency is approximately 10% to 30%; metabolic syndrome frequency is approximately 46%. Early lipid screening may also be considered as rates of dyslipidemia are higher in adolescents with Klinefelter syndrome compared to controls (e.g., lower high-density lipids, higher triglycerides). C
The risk of osteoporosis is high. There are no formal U.S. recommendations for screening, but bone density testing should be considered. C
The range of presentation is highly variable, and "textbook" cases represent only one end of a spectrum of disease severity. C
Small testicles and infertility are the most common physical/historical findings. C

Diagnosis is by cytogenetic analysis using karyotyping or chromosomal microarray analysis (XXY karyotype most commonly). Low testosterone level, elevated follicle-stimulating hormone and leuteinizing hormone levels, and azoospermia support the diagnosis. C
Klinefelter syndrome is underdiagnosed and most patients are diagnosed during or after the onset of puberty; average age at diagnosis is 25 years. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Normal or low follicle-stimulating hormone and leuteinizing hormone levels
Normal testicular size; usually fertile; normal hormone levels
Short stature, features of Turner syndrome
Muscle weakness and pain; myotonia; EKG abnormalities; family history
Exposure to toxins, specific medications, radiation, mumps; or chronic disease
Absence of physical features, normal cytogenetic analysis

list.listitem: The most common situation is a normal start of puberty followed by a slow progression of puberty with small testes and development of gynecomastia.

Findings are listed with their estimated frequencies, when available: infertility (nearly universal), small firm testes with 3 to 8 mL volume (95%-99%), decreased facial and body hair (88%), female pubic hair distribution (53%), abdominal adiposity, gynecomastia (27%), and taurodontism (enlargement of pulp and thinning of surface of teeth).
Patients also typically have narrow shoulders, broad hips, tall height, broad arm span, long lower body segment, and low weight for height.
Recurrent leg ulcerations may occur because of venous insufficiency and postthrombotic syndrome (13%).

On average, intelligence is slightly decreased, but this is highly variable. Patients commonly have delayed speech, decreased verbal reasoning ability, learning disabilities, and poor school performance.

There is also an increased risk of psychosocial problems and a high prevalence of psychiatric illness. Authors of a systematic review of 50 papers found language disorders and autism spectrum symptoms to be the most prevalent comorbidities in patients with Klinefelter syndrome.
Testicular size can be measured with orchidometer or ultrasound.

Chromosome analysis may be performed by cytogenetic analysis (karyotyping) of peripheral leukocytes or Barr body analysis of buccal epithelial cells. Cytogenetic analysis is the gold standard. Sensitivity is increased by increasing the cell count. When the diagnosis is suspected, Barr body analysis is 82% sensitive and 95% specific.

Chromosomal microarray analysis is a relatively new method to diagnose patients lacking an apparent syndromic phenotype. For this technique, the patient's DNA and a control DNA are labeled with different fluorescent dyes and then hybridized to a microarray chip containing thousands of DNA probes. The intensity of the fluorescent signals enables detection of deletions, duplications, or normal copy number variations in the patient's DNA.

Authors of a Cochrane review on non-invasive prenatal testing using massively parallel shotgun sequencing or targeted massively parallel sequencing of fetal circulating cell-free DNA for detecting fetal aneuploidies concluded that test performance was not sufficient to replace current invasive diagnostic testing.

Fluorescent in situ hybridization is the most sensitive and specific technique for diagnosing mosaicism. Barr body analysis is not sensitive for detecting mosaicism. Detection of mosaicism is important when assisted reproduction is of interest because these patients may have higher success with infertility interventions.
Semen analysis is helpful if future fertility is a concern, or cytogenetic analysis is not available. When the diagnosis is suspected, azoospermia is 93% sensitive (but only 38% specific).

Low serum total testosterone and high serum follicle-stimulating hormone and leuteinizing hormone levels support the diagnosis but are neither sensitive nor specific indicators. Many patients have testosterone levels at the lower end of the normal range and follicle-stimulating hormone and leuteinizing hormone levels at the upper end of the normal range.
Normal testosterone levels are highest in the morning and lowest at night, and progressively decline with age.

When Klinefelter syndrome is suspected, explore the fertility history and assess testicular size. Fertility is extraordinarily rare (although inaccurate assignment of paternity is not) and most patients have small firm testes (3-8 mL volume).
Azoospermia on semen analysis, low serum testosterone, and elevated follicle-stimulating hormone and leuteinizing hormone levels (beginning in the teenage years) support the diagnosis.
When diagnosis is suspected, perform chromosomal analysis.

Advisory booklets and informational websites on how to prepare and support patients and their families should be suggested as these may make it easier for parents to communicate with their child about their medical condition and the challenges they may encounter (e.g., https://www.dsdfamilies.org and https://www.dsdteens.org). It should be noted that gender role behavior, interests and preferences are mostly neither possible nor desirable to change and cannot be used to predict gender identity.
Testosterone supplementation is recommended for patients with hypogonadism, titrating dosage to maintain testosterone level in the middle of the normal range. B
Developmental evaluation and educational support are recommended for children. C
Cryopreservation of sperm should be performed in early adolescence. C
Patients should be advised of associated health risks and a surveillance plan created based on the patient’s needs and desires. C

Testosterone therapy is consistently recommended by experts, beginning between the ages of 11 and 13 years. The goal of therapy is to ensure that secondary sexual characteristics and maturation of the body and brain occur at a similar pace to peers.

If possible, testosterone therapy should be titrated to maintain serum testosterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and leuteinizing hormone levels in the middle of the normal range. In some patients, normalization of gonadotropins may not be possible. Titrating to symptoms should also be considered. In adolescents, appropriate dosage and serum testosterone level should be age-adjusted.

The Endo-European Reference Network 2022 guideline provides recommendations for congenital conditions associated with atypical chromosomal, gonadal or phenotypic sex development. They note that it is not clear if testosterone replacement should begin early, when LH starts to rise above normal levels (>+2 s.d.), or if testosterone supplementation should be postponed until testosterone levels fall below the normal range (<−2 s.d.). For patients with known Klinefelter syndrome, they state that pubertal induction can be started by age 12 years if there are no signs of pubertal development. In those with an identified cause of hypogonadism, puberty should be induced over a period of 2–4 years until a satisfactory outcome, usually when an adult dose has been reached.

A Swedish cost-effectiveness analysis found that lifelong testosterone depot injection therapy in patients with Klinefelter syndrome and hypogonadism was cost-effective with a gain of 1.67 quality-adjusted life-years at an incremental cost of 37,192 USD.
Testosterone increases body hair, increases penile length, and improves libido. It also improves bone density.

Testosterone may reverse gynecomastia, as well as reduce adiposity and increase muscle mass, although these findings have not been replicated in all studies. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that testosterone treatment in hypogonadal patients with Klinefelter syndrome improves body composition (e.g., reduces total body fat and total abdominal fat) and spinal bone density, but appears ineffective in ameliorating lipid and glycemic profiles.

Testosterone may improve mood, energy level, cognition, decision making, and social functioning, and may decrease aggression. Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 retrospective studies and 2 RCTs concluded that early androgen therapy improved behavioral functioning.
Testosterone may lower total cholesterol and normalize serum melatonin levels, and may possibly normalize hypercoagulability and facilitate remission of autoimmune disease.

Testosterone may not normalize the cardiovascular abnormalities found in patients with Klinefelter syndrome (e.g., abnormalities in left ventricular systolic and diastolic function and endothelial function). The chromosomal abnormality likely plays a significant role in inducing the cardiovascular phenotype in these patients.

In a nationwide registry-based matched cohort study, investigators found lower all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.56, 95%CI 0.37-0.85) in the 557 patients with Klinefelter syndrome treated with testosterone compared to the 950 untreated patients with Klinefelter syndrome born the same year; mortality rates for treated patients was comparable to that of the background population comparison cohort. In this study, the incidence of major cardiovascular events was similar between testosterone treated and untreated patients with Klinefelter syndrome.

Risks of testosterone therapy include erythrocytosis, progression of prostate cancer, worsening of aggressive tendencies, peliosis hepatitis, hepatic adenomas, hepatocellular carcinoma, and early bone maturation in children. In one study of testosterone gel, cough was the most common side effect. Adverse effects on several cardiovascular modulators have been described in vitro.

Various testosterone preparations are available and have been studied. Testosterone may be administered orally or by intramuscular injection, transdermal gel, transdermal patch, or subcutaneous pellets. Patches are often poorly tolerated, and dosage adjustments with subcutaneous pellets are problematic. Begin at the low end of the dosage range (ie, 50 mg testosterone enanthate every month, 10 mg transdermal testosterone every other day or 40 mg oral testosterone undecanoate daily) and then gradually increase to the adult dose.
There are few direct data addressing risks and benefits of testosterone therapy in prepubertal children with Klinefelter syndrome outside of the entity of microphallus.

In an RCT of 84 pre-pubertal boys with Klinefelter syndrome, low-dose androgen over 24 months compared to placebo resulted in benefit for only 1 of 5 primary endpoints (visual-motor function) but had positive effects on psychosocial function (i.e., anxiety, depression, and social problems) without significant effects on cognitive function, hyperactivity, or aggressive behaviors.

In a study of the influence of pubertal timing on adult health from sex-steroid exposure for patients with constitutional delay, Turner syndrome, and Klinefelter syndrome, authors found that earlier exposure was of benefit for bone mineral density but risks of prostate cancer and asthma were reduced with later exposure. In addition, later exposure was associated with lower BMI and blood pressure and higher educational attainment.

In a cross-sectional study of infants and toddlers with Klinefelter syndrome, hormone therapy administered by 12 months of age appeared to have a positive effect within the first year of life on auditory comprehension, expressive communication, receptive language, cognition, and motor development.

Gonadotropins can also be used for pubertal induction. Drugs tested in small studies include human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), human menopausal gonadotropin, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Authors of a systematic review found that gonadotropins induced significant increases in testicular volume, penile size, and testosterone in nearly all analyses. Higher spermatogenesis rates were observed with hCG + FSH (86%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 82%-91%) compared to hCG alone (40%, 95% CI 25%-56%) although study heterogeneity was high.
Gynecomastia may be corrected surgically, and satisfactory outcomes have been reported.
Consider neurodevelopmental evaluation, speech therapy, and educational support.
Preventive dental care is important because taurodontism increases the risk of tooth decay.
Consider echocardiogram to assess for mitral and aortic valve disease, which is common.
Maintain a high index of suspicion for thromboembolic disease, autoimmune disease, and mediastinal germ cell tumors, all of which are much more common in patients with Klinefelter syndrome.
Consider screening for osteoporosis.

If sperm is present on semen analysis and the patient is in his prechildbearing years, refer for cryopreservation of existing sperm. Surgical sperm retrieval rates based on the literature range from 28% to 70%. In the most recent systematic review including 48 studies with 2815 participants, the median sperm retrieval rate was 44% with no differences between adolescent and adult cohorts (45% vs. 42%).

The Endo-European Reference Network 2022 guidelines suggest performing sperm analysis if possible before the start of testosterone treatment based on a theoretical concern that testosterone preparations may suppress any remaining spermatogenesis if the endogenous LH drive is reduced.

Authors of a meta-analysis found that even in patients negative for spermatozoa, 26 of the 56 (46.4%) peripubertal/adolescent and 37 of 152 (24.3%) adult patients were positive for spermatogonia (undifferentiated male germ cells). In this study, spermatogonial cells were present in all fetuses and infants, 83% of the prepubertal patients' testes, and 42.7% and 48.5% of peripubertal and adult groups.
Authors of a systematic review found sperm retrieval rates of 50% after testicular sperm extraction for patients with Klinefelter syndrome; pregnancy and live birth rates were also about 50%.
In a meta-analysis including 22 studies, authors did not find benefit of pre-treatment hormone therapy on surgical sperm retrieval among in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

Risks of testicular sperm extraction (TESE) among men with Klinefelter syndrome and men with non-obstructive azoospermia include a transient decrease in total testosterone levels at 6 months (mean decrease of 4.1 and 2.7 nmol/l, respectively) with recovery to baseline levels at 26 and 18 months after TESE, respectively, based on a meta-analysis of 15 studies. In one of those studies, there was an increased risk of erectile dysfunction related to decreased total testosterone levels 6 months after extraction.

Embryos are at increased risk for cytogenetic abnormalities. In 1 study of sperm from 5 patients with nonmosaic Klinefelter, 93.7% of sperms were normal; the remaining 6.3% of sperms had sex chromosome abnormalities. In another study of 28 embryos from nonmosaic Klinefelter couples, 17.8% had sex chromosome abnormalities.

Fertility treatment may be offered using testicular sperm extraction or testicular fine needle aspiration and intracytoplasmic sperm injection. "Healthy" appearing embryos are selected, and couples are typically offered preimplantation genetic diagnosis to assure that a healthy embryo is implanted.
Consultation with an endocrinologist may be helpful when titrating doses of testosterone in pediatric patients.
Individuals with untreated Klinefelter syndrome have increased mortality compared with the general population.
Infertility treatment options exist, although success is limited. B

Testosterone supplementation may increase body hair, increase penis size, improve libido, reverse gynecomastia, improve muscle mass, and reduce adiposity; improve cognition, mood and social functioning, and decrease aggression; B and improve bone density. B

Authors of a systematic review including 13 studies found poorer quality of life among patients with Klinefelter syndrome, with associated impairments in physical, psychological, level independence and social relationship domains.

Total testosterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and leuteinizing hormone levels are typically assessed monthly during initial therapy. Liver function tests and hematocrit should also be monitored. Prostate-specific antigen monitoring and serial prostate examination is suggested in older men. Monitoring bone maturation is recommended in children, and consultation with an endocrinologist may be helpful.
Prenatal diagnosis is possible with karyotyping of cells obtained by amniocentesis.
Increased maternal age increases the risk of conception of a fetus with Klinefelter syndrome.
Parents should be counseled about the highly variable phenotypic range of Klinefelter syndrome.
Fetuses with Klinefelter syndrome have a slightly increased risk of spontaneous abortion.

Infants have no specific clinical features, but on average have a smaller head circumference, lower weight, and longer length. They have an increased incidence of congenital abnormalities, undescended testes, and micropenis. Micropenis has been treated with topical or intramuscular testosterone.
Although highly variable, physical findings in children may include increased height, small penis size, and small testicles.
Seventy seven percent of children have difficulty learning to read and 42% have delayed speech. Children are at high risk of poor school performance and need close monitoring and educational support.
Children with Klinefelter syndrome are more likely to require psychiatric care.
Children may be at an increased risk of fractures.
Testosterone therapy is recommended beginning in adolescence, between the ages of 11 and 13 years. Monitoring bone maturation is suggested and consultation with an endocrinologist may be helpful.

Infertility is rapidly progressive during adolescence and early adulthood. Sperm collection and cryopreservation should be performed in early adolescence when the diagnosis is known. Testosterone therapy does not prevent infertility.
